entries.exactPassage: Key idea: Thabo was afraid of the conversation. But not talking was worse. The paradox: difficult conversations are like medicine. Unpleasant in the moment. Healing in the long run. Avoidance is not kindness. It is cowardice dressed up as care.
entries.concern: Calling avoidance cowardice and difficult conversations healing can shame someone appropriately avoiding an unsafe encounter.
entries.proposedWording: For an ordinary resolvable disagreement, careful preparation and a conversation may help. Delaying or declining unsafe contact, seeking support or writing the unsent letter can be appropriate.

entries.exactPassage: Here’s the tension: the conversation might not go well. Sipho Jr. might have gotten angry. The outcome is not guaranteed. The only thing guaranteed is that avoidance guarantees failure. And Atlehang Ngwenya's grandmother was right: fear is a storyteller, and most of its stories are lies. Thabo's fear told him Sipho Jr. would quit. The truth was that Sipho Jr. was struggling and needed help.
entries.concern: The passage acknowledges uncertain outcomes but then says avoidance guarantees failure and most fear is false. Fear can indicate a genuine threat.
entries.proposedWording: A prepared conversation may help in an ordinary safe disagreement, but outcomes are uncertain. Distinguish a prediction from evidence and take safety concerns seriously; seek appropriate support when needed.

entries.exactPassage: If you genuinely cannot have the conversation this week, write a letter to the person explaining what you would say. You do not have to send it. But be honest: is there a real reason you cannot have it — or are you just afraid?
entries.concern: The unsent-letter alternative is useful but its closing question implies fear is not a real reason, undermining appropriate boundaries.
entries.proposedWording: If contact is unsuitable, unsafe or not possible, write an unsent letter to practise the preparation. Consider what support or information would help; you do not have to contact the person.

entries.exactPassage: Story 3 — Failure and Mentorship: "Our first business failed. I felt like a failure. Then my mentor — a lecturer who believed in me — said: 'You did not fail. You paid tuition. Now learn the lesson. If you quit now, the tuition is wasted.' I did not quit. The second business is still running. Small. But real."
entries.concern: The tuition metaphor is legitimate, but the assertion that quitting wastes it can encourage persisting with an unworkable or harmful venture.
entries.proposedWording: Keep the tuition metaphor and Themba’s account, while clarifying that using a lesson may mean continuing, redesigning, seeking help or stopping; the next venture is not guaranteed to succeed.
entries.implementationImpact: Separate reviewed learner-source wording proposal. Retain lesson, block, prompt and response identities through explicit compiler mapping before any source release; no source change in this batch.

entries.exactPassage: Here’s the tension: the tuition is only worth it if you learn the lesson. Many people fail and learn nothing. They blame others. They quit. The tuition is wasted. The people who fail and learn — who extract the lesson, who adjust, who try again — turn failure into an investment.
entries.concern: The passage links quitting with blame and wasted learning, excluding responsible stopping and constraints beyond the person’s control.
entries.proposedWording: Learning from a setback can guide a different attempt, a redesign or a decision to stop. Some losses reflect external constraints; reflection takes time and does not make harm necessary or worthwhile.

entries.exactPassage: "You are learning to be leaders. That means you need to understand the legal side of leadership. Because the law does not care about your good intentions. It cares about what you did — and what you failed to do."
entries.category: Legal inaccuracy requiring qualified South African review
entries.concern: The repeated absolute that law does not care about intention is inaccurate across legal contexts. Goodwill is not an automatic exemption, but intention may matter.
entries.proposedWording: Good intentions do not automatically remove legal responsibility. The relevance of intention, actions and omissions depends on the applicable law and facts; seek appropriate qualified advice for a real situation.
entries.implementationImpact: Separate reviewed learner-source wording proposal. Retain lesson, block, prompt and response identities through explicit compiler mapping before any source release; no source change in this batch.

entries.exactPassage: Fiduciary duty: "If you manage money for others — a cooperative, a business, even a family stokvel — you have a legal duty to act in their best interest. Not yours. Theirs."
entries.category: Role-dependent legal claim requiring qualified review

entries.proposedWording: Managing another person’s money can carry serious duties. Whether fiduciary duties apply, and what they require, depends on the role, facts and applicable law; obtain appropriate advice.

entries.exactPassage: Here’s the tension: the section you are avoiding is the section that will teach you the most. If you are avoiding the ethical framework, it is because you have not faced a real dilemma yet — or because you have, and you did not handle it well. The gaps in your philosophy are the gaps in your leadership. Face them now. Not later.
entries.concern: Avoiding the ethics section does not establish that a learner has never faced a dilemma or handled it badly. Privacy, uncertainty, language and time are other reasons.
entries.proposedWording: A difficult section may point to a question worth exploring. Identify what makes it hard, choose suitable examples and seek support without assuming a personal or moral failure.

entries.exactPassage: Question 3 — The Authenticity Test: Read your draft philosophy out loud to yourself. Now ask: If someone found this document in 20 years, would they know it was written by YOU — specifically you, with your experiences, your voice, your scars? If not, what needs to change? Write the one sentence that is most authentically yours.
entries.category: Disclosure pressure within a legitimate authenticity metaphor
entries.concern: The voice/scars imagery is a legitimate perspective, but the test can imply intimate hardship is necessary to demonstrate authenticity.
entries.proposedWording: Use your own words and an appropriate specific experience to explain a principle. Ordinary experiences count, and private or painful details do not have to be disclosed.

entries.exactPassage: Here’s the tension: the things that move you are mirrors — they show you what you value. The things that irritate you are also mirrors — they show you what you fear or reject in yourself. Every philosophy presented today is a lens through which you can see yourself more clearly.
entries.concern: The mirror metaphor is legitimate, but irritation is asserted to reveal fear or a rejected part of oneself. Different values, boundaries and context can also explain a response.
entries.proposedWording: Resonance or discomfort can invite reflection. Consider different possible reasons, including a disagreement or boundary, without assuming a hidden fear or defect.

entries.exactPassage: Question 3 — The Mirror Question: Which presentation made you uncomfortable — and why? Discomfort is data. What is the discomfort telling you about your own leadership gaps?
entries.concern: The prompt presumes both discomfort and a leadership gap; a reasoned difference or absence of discomfort is also valid.
entries.proposedWording: If a presentation made you uncomfortable, consider why. It may raise a question, a difference, a boundary or something to develop; no discomfort or private disclosure is required.

entries.exactPassage: 9. The 1-10 Scale: At the start of the term, you were a "1" on the leadership literacy scale. Where are you now, honestly? What is the exact number? What is the ONE specific thing you need to do in Term 3 to move up by a single point?
entries.concern: The prompt assumes every learner began at one and implies a comparable exact leadership-literacy score. No validated scale or shared baseline is established.
entries.proposedWording: Using your own earlier reflection if available, describe where you now see a strength or a question. Any rating is a personal reflective estimate, not a grade; identify a feasible next step without assuming a starting score.
